title: The Shutdown Fortnight: Why the Quietest Two Weeks of the Year Are Often the Most Expensive
linkedin:
Shutdown dates just went out to your team for Christmas. Most owners have not yet worked out what those two quiet weeks actually cost.

Trading stops, but almost nothing else does. Rent keeps moving. Loan and equipment finance repayments stay on schedule. Software subscriptions renew whether anyone is logged in or not. And if the shutdown is being used to clear annual leave balances, which it often is, that payout lands in the same weeks as well, a wage cost concentrated into exactly the fortnight revenue has stopped.

The gap rarely ends when the office reopens either. Clients are usually closed over the same weeks, so invoices sent in early December often sit unpaid until accounts payable teams are back at their desks in late January. A two week shutdown can easily become a six or seven week cash gap once you count the receivables lag on the other side.

None of this is a sign anything has gone wrong. It is simply what a deliberate pause in trading costs, and it is entirely plannable once the number is known.

Mid September, when shutdown dates get locked in, is exactly the right time to size that number too. Work out what goes out during the break, line it up against a realistic view of when December invoices will actually clear, and decide ahead of time whether to hold a buffer or draw on a facility on your own terms rather than under pressure in the third week of December.
